lessons.title: You Only Get Four Thousand Weeks
lessons.key_idea: An average life lasts about four thousand weeks, and facing that limit honestly is the starting point for using time well.

lessons.title: The Efficiency Trap
lessons.key_idea: Getting through tasks faster rarely frees you, because doing more usually just attracts more to do, like an inbox that refills as you empty it.

lessons.title: Choose What to Neglect
lessons.key_idea: Since you can never do everything, the real skill is deliberately deciding which important things you will fail at so you can focus on what matters most.

lessons.title: Why We Reach for Distraction
lessons.key_idea: Distraction is often an escape from the discomfort of facing hard, limited, uncertain work, so the cure is accepting that discomfort rather than relying only on willpower or apps.

lessons.title: Stop Living for the Future
lessons.key_idea: Treating every moment as a means to some future payoff robs you of life now, so value activities like rest and hobbies for their own sake.

lessons.title: The Power of Patience
lessons.key_idea: Meaningful work and change unfold at their own pace, so staying with something through its slow, unoriginal early stages is what eventually leads somewhere distinctive.

lessons.title: Embrace Your Cosmic Insignificance
lessons.key_idea: Accepting that your life is tiny on a cosmic scale, and that time is best shared with others, frees you from impossible standards to do modest things that truly matter.

plan.title: Four Thousand Weeks
plan.author: Oliver Burkeman
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core arguments and main examples well, though I may not recall every minor anecdote precisely.
plan.one_liner: You get roughly four thousand weeks of life. Stop trying to fit everything in, and start choosing.
plan.summary: Oliver Burkeman, a former productivity enthusiast, argues that most time management advice rests on an impossible promise: that with enough efficiency, we can finally get on top of everything. The average human life lasts only about four thousand weeks, and no system can make that enough for all our ambitions. Worse, becoming more efficient often just brings more demands. Drawing on philosophy and psychology, Burkeman suggests a different path: accept your limits, make hard choices about what to neglect, and stop treating the present as a mere stepping stone to some future moment of control. He explores why we flee into distraction, why patience is a superpower, why rest needs no justification, and why time is richer when shared with others. The result is a liberating, deeply humane guide to spending a finite life well.
